title: Say what the data says
summary: Chart a week of step counts, make one claim, and say it out loud in 60 seconds.

steps.title: One claim, one chart, one sentence of doubt
steps.body:
A claim backed by data needs three parts. One claim: a single sentence about what the numbers actually show. One chart: something to point at while you say it, so people can check it for themselves instead of trusting your memory. One sentence of doubt: one honest reason your claim might not tell the whole story, like a day you forgot to wear the badge.

The question of the week is: is more always better? Think about your step count while you plan your talk: is walking more steps every single day actually a good goal, or could there be a day where fewer steps was the right amount. Use your answer to the question as the ending of your talk.

steps.title: Chart your circuit and make a claim
steps.body: Chart something you counted this week on graph paper, one bar for each item. The best source is your bug diary from the breadboard build: how many tries each stage took before it worked, the LED alone, the resistor, the button, the code. If you kept any other daily count this week, that works too. Look at the chart and make one claim about what it shows, for example 'the button took the most tries because of the wiring.' Say the claim in 60 seconds, holding the chart up so people can see it. Practise saying it twice with a timer running.
checklist: Chart shows one bar for each stage or each day you counted
Claim is one sentence backed by the chart, not a guess
Talk stays under 60 seconds and includes one honest doubt about the data

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the talk. Phone propped up, whole face in frame, chart visible.
